Back when Intel launched its Panther Lake laptop chips at CES 2026 , I knew they were going to find their way into handhelds at some point, and I'm glad they did. While I do have gripes with the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, mostly relating to its large size and my tiny hands, this is an absolute behemoth of a handheld gaming PC. This is the first handheld from a mainstream PC manufacturer that I can actually turn some settings up in games like Crimson Desert and Cyberpunk, while still getting decent frame rates. Now, if only it came with an OLED display.

Incredible performance for a handheld. The MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ is one of the first handhelds I've tested with the new Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip. And, it blows the AMD Ryzen Z2 Extreme out of the water. The Claw 8 EX AI+ is the same price as the Legion Go 2 right now, but it is up to 55% faster, just 8 months after Lenovo's handheld hit the market. Finally, we get a handheld that can run AAA games at more than minimum settings.

Beautiful 8-inch display, but with a catch. The MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ uses the same 8-inch 1200p display as last year's Claw 8 AI+, and that's not a bad thing. This is a gorgeous LCD panel that gets super bright with excellent color accuracy. However, the Claw 8 AI+ was, like, $1000, the Claw 8 EX AI+ is $1799. I know that mostly comes down to the RAM crisis we're all going through, but I still want an OLED panel if I'm paying that much.

Made for large hands. I have pretty small hands, so I do struggle a bit with the Claw 8 EX AI+ sometimes. The menu buttons directly to the left and right of the display are a little bit of a chore to press, as I have to stretch my thumb a bit to hit them. However, if you have larger hands this is going to be a non-issue for you.

Multi-frame generation in a handheld. Love it or hate it, frame generation is here to stay. And, thanks to the Intel chip in the Claw 8 EX AI+, this handheld has access to multi-frame generation, up to 4x. You still want to avoid turning it on if you're not already getting 30-40 fps already, but it does help you take full advantage of the 120Hz display that's built-in.

For years, the Steam Machine was my budget pick, but those days are over, at least for now. Ever since Valve raised the price on its handhelds, the base, white Asus ROG Xbox Ally has become the budget champ, with comparable performance to Valve's handheld, but at a lower price point. However, it does still come with Windows, which does hold it back a bit, but that's nothing a Bazzite or SteamOS installation can't fix.

Affordable in the age of the RAMpocalypse. It's no secret that gaming hardware has been skyrocketing in price this year, due to the ongoing RAM crisis. But somehow, Asus has managed to avoid raising the price on the base ROG Xbox Ally so far. It's still a $599 handheld, which seemed steep when it first came out, but after the Steam Deck went up in price earlier this year, it seems like a bargain now.

There are compromises, like with any budget option. When I was testing the Xbox Ally, I found that it was drastically slower than handhelds with the Z2 Extreme processor. In Cyberpunk 2077, with the high preset at the native 1080p resolution, and with FSR set to Quality, I only got 22 fps, compared to 44 fps from the Xbox Ally X with the same settings. That seems bad, but keep in mind that it's nearly half the price.

Battery life with the best of them. Current generation handheld gaming PCs seem like they're stuck at around two and a half hours of battery life, and the Xbox Ally is no different. Playing Cyberpunk 2077 at its default power profile of 15W, I got about 2 hours and 31 minutes of gameplay before the Ally shut down. It would have been nice if Asus could have used the same 80WHr battery it stuck in the Xbox Ally X, if only to stretch the battery a bit more. But, hey, that probably would have raised the price a bit.

Still one of the most comfortable handhelds out there. Both the Xbox Ally and the most powerful Xbox Ally X are the most comfortable handhelds to actually hold and play. And because of the less powerful hardware, the white Xbox Ally actually gets an edge, because its a bit lighter, which means less wrist strain over long gaming sessions.

articles.title: Supreme’s 2026 Fall/Winter Collection Features a 24K Gold Analogue Pocket
articles.summary: Streetwear brand Supreme has unveiled its Fall/Winter 2026 collection, and it features a collab with Analogue Pocket, the fantastic retro handheld that lets you play your Game Boy cartridges on FPGA-based hardware. Also in the collection is a Supreme-branded Dyson Vacuum, Kodak Super-8 Camera, and a galvanized steel mailbox, all bright red, of course.
articles.body:
Streetwear brand Supreme has unveiled its Fall/Winter 2026 collection , and it features a collab with Analogue Pocket, the fantastic retro handheld that lets you play your Game Boy cartridges on FPGA-based hardware.

Also in the collection is a Supreme-branded Dyson Vacuum, Kodak Super-8 Camera, and a galvanized steel mailbox, all bright red, of course.

The Analogue Pocket collab actually comes in two variants: one the standard Supreme red, as well as a second that's plated in 24K gold. As for the underlying Analogue Pocket itself, it's the same high-end retro handheld we loved in our review , which my colleague Seth noted "solves the limitations of classic handhelds with a familiar but distinct style you don't find with emulation-based solutions."

The Pocket uses an FPGA solution, short for "field-programmable gate arrays," which means it replicates the Game Boy and Game Boy Advance's original electronic hardware "at the transistor level." In other words, games are played on actual hardware, rather than being emulated, so every game – from Kirby Tilt n' Tumble's original motion controls to Perfect Dark's AAA-powered rumble pak – runs exactly as it was originally intended.

"Simply put," Seth said, "it's the best possible way to enjoy your handheld gaming collection."

The standard edition Analogue Pocket retails for $239.99 , though it comes in limited quantities and typically sells out quickly whenever units become available. There's no word yet how much the new Supreme-branded variant will cost, but it will undoubtedly be even more limited edition. The 24K gold version, even more so. Is it practical? No. Do I care at all about Supreme? Not a bit. Do I still want it? Absolutely.

For other, likely less expensive ways to play your games on the go, be sure to check our guide to the best handheld gaming PCs .

Bo Moore is IGN's Senior Manager of Tech. You can find him online @usebomswisely.

articles.title: GPU Swapping Spree Halted After Suspected Thieves Lose Power During Esports Hotel Heist
articles.summary: They would have gotten away with it, too, if it weren't for that meddling electrician.
articles.body:
Thanks to AI data center demand, reasonably-priced GPUs are still hard to come by . Maybe not, though, if you find the right seller and don't ask too many questions. Like maybe the two men accused of harvesting Nvidia RTX 5080s from in-room gaming PCs of esports hotel rooms in China, replacing them with less-powerful RTX 3060s, then reselling the stolen ones for around half their market value, according to VideoCardz .

The two might've gotten away with the alleged caper, but on July 18, they lost power to their room and requested to be moved to a different unit. Later, an electrician investigating the issue found pry marks on the room's gaming PC case. Staff soon discovered the GPUs had been replaced in both rooms.

Local police arrested the two in the Guangbutun computer district on July 20 with two unsold, apparently stolen GPUs still in their possession, wrote Tom's Hardware in its own story about the heist . The outlet says police reported the suspects had admitted to carrying out the same crime four other times, and adds that "the total loss reported from their GPU-swapping spree was 80,000 Yuan, or almost $12,000."

According to Tom's, other victimized hotels didn't catch on because the PCs "ran just fine, and there were no complaints from later customers, so there was no reason to inspect them up close."

Wes is a freelance writer (Freelance Wes, they call him) who has covered technology, gaming, and entertainment steadily since 2020 at Gizmodo, Tom's Hardware, Hardcore Gamer, and most recently, The Verge. Inside of him there are two wolves: one that thinks it wouldn't be so bad to start collecting game consoles again, and the other who also thinks this, but more strongly.

articles.title: The Best Pixel 11 Cases to Protect Your New Phone
articles.summary: Pixelsnap your way into fall damage protection, with rugged, clear, and leather options for your new phone.
articles.body:
Google has announced this year’s crop of Pixel phones, the Pixel 11 line , and they’re more powerful, more expensive, and of course, your old Pixel 10 or earlier cases may not fit them. Even if they do, the buttons might not line up or your old case might be a little worse for the wear these days. So, it’s time to hunt for a new outer shell for your phone .

Right after a phone launches is usually the hardest time to get a case that you can count on – most third-party case makers haven’t gotten their hands on the phones, and even if they kept an eye on leaks, there’s the chance that what they make won’t really fit right.

It’s different with Google, which seems to be a little looser with its phones’ designs. The company has partnered with some of the most well-known third-party manufacturers and is already selling their cases on the Google Store. As such, all of my preferred cases come straight from there, this time.

OtterBox Commuter Series Case with Pixelsnap

Google Pixelsnap Case for Pixel 11 Pro Fold

Google’s first-party offering is its Pixelsnap Case. The company sells these for all three of the mainline Pixel 11 phones, and in several colors to boot. There is, of course, a black option for all phones, but if you’re feeling more adventurous, you can find these cases in a salmony pink, an olive green, and light blue for the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, as well as a light purple, a very in-your-face pink, and a pistachio green.

These cases feature a built-in magnet for those who want to take advantage of the phones’ upgrade to 25W wireless charging. Being made by Google, you can assume these cases will fit your phone just fine. The only drawbacks are that silicone can be a little too grippy, and at $50, they’re not the cheapest case you can find.

Dbrand has been the best option for designer cases for some time now. The company has a ton of fun options that range from simple colors to trippy designs to printed photos and scans of the internals of the very phones they protect. They also feature a grippy, textured outer edge to help you keep your handset, well, in hand. And, each one has a magnetic ring for Qi2 wireless charging.

Dbrand claims they’re “the most precise fit on earth.” I don’t always take the company at its word when it makes hyperbolic statements like that, but in its favor is that you can buy the Grip case straight from Google. Unfortunately, these cases don’t come cheap – they’re either $55 or $60, depending on which design you choose. Interestingly, the fancier cases are ever so slightly cheaper when you buy from the Google Store , where they’re available for $59. But you’d have to really like the “Sketch” or “Ultramatte Teardown” designs, because those are the only ones Google is selling.

OtterBox is my longtime go-to for a beefy, smartphone-protecting case, and the company is quick on the draw with its cases for the Pixel 11 series. I’ve always found its Commuter cases to be a nice compromise versus its Defender ones, which feature a dual-layer design but add a huge amount of bulk to the equation. The Commuter series won’t feel thin in hand, but they tend to still fit in your pants pockets (as long as your pockets aren’t tiny).

The Pixel 11 cases feature a magnetic ring for wireless charging, which is nice, and, at least according to the options on the Google Store, the one for the standard 11 fits the 11 Pro as well. Odd, considering they have slightly different dimensions – the Pixel 11 Pro is 0.1 – 0.2mm smaller in each direction – but OtterBox cases have never done me wrong in the past.

My favorite leather phone case maker, Bullstrap, doesn’t do Pixel phones, and neither does my usual second choice, Ryan London. But Bellroy has received solid reviews for years for its Pixel cases, and it features aluminum buttons and a magnet for Qi2 wireless charging. It helps that at $60 (or $55 on the Google Store ), they’re more affordable than the ones typically made by either of those companies.

There are things to note about Bellroy, though – I’ve seen complaints that its leather, while good, doesn’t feel quite as premium as those by the companies I mentioned above. A reviewer at 9to5Toys noted their Pixel 9 Bellroy leather case almost feels rubbery, rather than fine-grained. Also, there’s no tan option for the base Pixel 11. That said, they were created in partnership with Google, so they should give a guaranteed fit.

Dbrand makes this list again because its clear Ghost case lets you show off your Pixel phone without the yellow-prone clear TPU that most clear cases are made of. Yes, that means you won’t be able to totally pretend you’ve become one of the bold caseless phone users out there, but at least you won’t have to buy a new case in six months when it starts looking like an aging Super Nintendo.

Plus, Dbrand’s case is $60. That’s a lot, yes, but it’s also cheaper than Mous’s clear case option, which features a similar design but costs $70, instead. If you need to go cheaper, you could take a chance on Gorilla Cases, which makes a $40 one with what looks like the same approach, and it features a kickstand. (Gorilla doesn’t make the official list because I have no direct experience with its cases, and there are alternatives with which I have.)

With folding phones, you need to be a little choosier about the case you stick on them. You can imagine how a bad fit can mean a weirdly floppy front screen bumper or an annoying hinge. So for that, I recommend going with Google’s first-party Pixelsnap case.

This year’s case features an integrated hinge cover, unlike last year’s. It also has a magnetic ring so you can wirelessly charge your phone using a magnetic puck or mount-style charger. The case is made of soft-touch material like the other Pixelsnap cases, too. It’s pricey, though, at $80, and it only comes in two colors: black and green.

Make sure the case has a magnetic ring. Do you like to watch content and don’t always want to be holding your phone while you do it? Get one with a kickstand. Care about button feel? Maybe avoid the ones without metal buttons.

Normally, right out of the gate, I would say go with the first-party case option if you can swing it. It’s usually the one most likely to have a good fit and offer solid protection, after all. But those can be pricey. Plus, as I wrote at the top of this page and as my list shows, Google has partnered with a number of case makers for the Pixel 11 series. As such, there’s a good number of third-party options available to you in the Google Store. I picked the ones I like for this list, but realistically, you could go with anything available in the Google Store that appeals to you and be fine.

If you’re patient and you really care about buying the best case the first time, the right thing to do is familiarize yourself with case reviewers. Find the ones who prioritize as many of the same things as you do, and see what they recommend. Barring that, I say again: go with something made by a company you know and trust.

Inside of him there are two wolves: one that thinks it wouldn't be so bad to start collecting game consoles again, and the other who also thinks this, but more strongly.
paragraphs: Google has announced this year’s crop of Pixel phones, the Pixel 11 line , and they’re more powerful, more expensive, and of course, your old Pixel 10 or earlier cases may not fit them. Even if they do, the buttons might not line up or your old case might be a little worse for the wear these days. So, it’s time to hunt for a new outer shell for your phone .

Right after a phone launches is usually the hardest time to get a case that you can count on – most third-party case makers haven’t gotten their hands on the phones, and even if they kept an eye on leaks, there’s the chance that what they make won’t really fit right.

It’s different with Google, which seems to be a little looser with its phones’ designs. The company has partnered with some of the most well-known third-party manufacturers and is already selling their cases on the Google Store. articles.title: gamescom 2026: How to Watch and Daily Schedule of the Biggest Gaming Event
articles.summary: IGN is live from Cologne, Germany for gamescom 2026! Here's all the info you need on how to watch the live shows, the schedule of events, and what to expect.
articles.body:
Gamescom is back for 2026! IGN is the official partner and will be broadcasting live from Cologne, Germany August 25–30 with live coverage of everything from developer interviews to show floor demos to exclusive trailers and gameplay from incredible upcoming games, along with so much more. Read on below for all the information you need to get excited for the big event!

gamescom takes place Tuesday, August 25–August 30 in Cologne, Germany.

gamescom Opening Night Live (with Official Pre-Show and IGN Post-Show) - 10:30am PT / 1:30pm ET / 7:30pm CEST

Opening Night Live (ONL) is back for 2026. This in-person event will be livestreamed and kicks off the beginning of gamescom! Tune in and check out big trailers, gameplays, and tons of news reveals throughout the night.

ONL will have a 30-minute pre-show prior to the main show, which will run for about two hours. Immediately following Opening Night Live, IGN will be breaking down all the biggest reveals from the show in our own deep-dive ONL post-show!

IGN gamescom studio Day 1 - 6am PT / 9am ET / 3pm CEST

Day 1 of IGN’s live coverage will feature developer interviews, exclusive reveals, and much more from games including:

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Songs of the Past

TARAE: The Unbound (Potentially Trinca Host)

Xbox Day 1 livestream - 7am PDT / 10am EDT / 3pm BST / 4pm CEST

Xbox will have special guests on their livestream, gameplay reveals, trailers, and more.

IGN gamescom studio Day 2 - 6am PT / 9am ET / 3pm CEST

Day 2 of IGN’s live coverage will feature more developer interviews, exclusive trailers and reveals, and more from the games below:

Xbox Day 2 livestream - 7am PDT / 10am EDT / 3pm BST / 4pm CEST

Xbox’s livestream will have more interviews and special guests, new trailers, and gameplay.

gamescom award show and gamescom studio Day 3 6am PT / 9am ET / 3pm CEST

The gamescom Award Show is back for 2026 and IGN is hosting it once again! We will be celebrating all the winners, and full list will be published on IGN.com , along with more reveals in the livestream from the following games:

IGN gamescom studio Day 4 - 6am PT / 9am ET / 3pm CEST

Day 4 of IGN’s live coverage will feature more exclusive reveals and developer interviews from games including:

IGN gamescom studio Day 5 - 6am PT / 9am ET / 3pm CEST

Day 5 of IGN’s live coverage will feature fun conversations and deep-dives with IGN's podcast crews and some game reveals from the following:

Here’s the full list of places you can watch the gamescom livestreams:

Fans can look forward to seeing live developer interviews, exclusive reveals, gameplay, and deep-dives, from Control Resonant, Dune: Awakening, Crimson Desert, Fable, Persona 4 Revival, Alien: Isolation 2, Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, and many more!

Xbox will have have a huge booth at gamescom, with 140 gaming stations featuring 25 upcoming games, including Fable, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Alien: Isolation 2, Stranger Than Heaven, Gears of War: E-Day, Minecraft Dungeons II, Metro 2039, and more. Developers will also be there to meet players and make the experience that much better.

Stay tuned to IGN for everything gamescom 2026 as all the reveals drop!

Jessie Wade is Associate Director of Editorial Programming at IGN. You can find her playing cozy games on her Switch these days or getting way too into Elder Scrolls Online.

articles.title: Marvel’s Wolverine Limited-Edition PS5, DualSense Controller, and Console Covers Are Up for Preorder
articles.summary: Marvel's Wolverine for PS5 is getting the royal treatment, with limited-edition PS5 consoles, covers, and controllers up for preorder now.
articles.body:
Update 11:56 a.m. ET: The controller is now live on Amazon , but not the console bundle. These items are selling out quickly. If you want one and you see it in stock, grab it before it's gone.

Marvel’s Wolverine comes out on September 15, and on that same day Sony is also releasing a handful of new Wolverine-themed pieces of PlayStation 5 hardware. There’s a limited-edition PS5 Digital Edition bundle, some console covers, and a DualSense Wireless Controller, all decked out in black and either classic “Battle Yellow” or “Adamantium” white. They're all available for preorder on PlayStation Direct , with the controller and console bundle available at a handful of other retailers. Read on for the details.

DualSense Wireless Controller – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition

PlayStation 5 Digital Edition – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition Bundle

DualSense Wireless Controller – Marvel’s Wolverine Adamantium Limited Edition

PlayStation 5 Console Covers – Battle Yellow Limited Edition

PlayStation 5 Pro Console Covers – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition

PlayStation 5 Pro Console Covers – Marvel’s Wolverine Adamantium Limited Edition

For those with no time to read blurbs, you can scroll through the catalog above to find the Wolverine-themed hardware for you.

The Battle Yellow controller is bold and very “Wolverine-y.” I love it. It features three jagged yellow claw slashes across the touchpad and left grip, with some gray weathering on either side. The sticks and bottom portion of the controller are yellow, as are the shapes on the face buttons and the directions on the D-pad.

PS5 Digital Edition – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition Bundle

If you want a new PS5, you can preorder this bundle, which includes the Wolverine-themed PS5 Digital console, plus the yellow-and-black controller, plus a digital code for Marvel’s Wolverine.

The console has an etching of the X-Men hero’s angry, yelling face at the top, with a triple slash going diagonally down the side of the machine. The whole thing is yellow and black, just like Wolverine’s costume. The controller is the same one available separately (see above).

DualSense Wireless Controller – Marvel’s Wolverine Adamantium Limited Edition (PS Direct Exclusive)

This metallic white color scheme is inspired by Wolverine's alloy-infused skeleton. It's also a PS Direct exclusive in the US and the UK , or Smyths Toys in Ireland for €84.99.

PS5 Console Covers – Battle Yellow Limited Edition (PS Direct Exclusive)

Anyone who already has a PS5 Slim can pick up a set of Wolverine-themed console covers instead of buying the whole bundle. The standard PS5 console covers come with all the pieces you need to deck out your Slim PS5, regardless of whether you have the digital or disc edition.

PS5 Pro Console Covers – Marvel’s Wolverine Battle Yellow Limited Edition (PS Direct Exclusive)

If you have a PS5 Pro and you like the look of the yellow design, you can get these console covers. It includes panels for the standard digital console, as well as the disc drive attachment.

PS5 Pro Console Covers – Marvel’s Wolverine Adamantium Limited Edition (PS Direct Exclusive)

If you have a PS5 Pro and you don’t care for yellow (or just prefer your gaming hardware to come in more muted hues), you can pick up this set of console covers that are metallic white instead of yellow.

And of course if you want to play the game at launch, you can preorder it, too. Check out our Marvel’s Wolverine preorder guide for full details on what comes in each edition.

Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

articles.title: The Strange New Worlds Puppet Episode Feels Like It Got Here 20 Years Too Late
articles.summary: The puppet episode of Strange New Worlds feels like it got here 20 years too late, with Ethan Peck’s non-puppet Spock standing tall as the hour’s saving grace.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 5, “Level Five Transporter Accident.”

Alright then, the puppet episode is finally here.

We’ve known this one was coming ever since it was first teased, what, two San Diego Comic-Cons ago ? The latest in high-concept Strange New Worlds episodes – this directly follows the zany Hangover riff from two weeks ago, and last week’s film noir homage – “Level Five Transporter Accident” certainly does feel like an accident… but not one that can be fixed with mere needle and thread the way the puppets here can. Indeed, its only saving grace is the performance from the always reliable Ethan Peck as Spock, who manages to walk the line between comedic Vulcan acting and conflicted Vulcan acting just fine.

When Scotty (Martin Quinn) tries to push his transporter tech to its limits – a nice nod to the Kelvinverse movies, where that Scotty (Simon Pegg) makes some big leaps with the old beam ‘em up technology – things go awry. Since he’s using his childhood puppet “Little Ricky” as a test subject, when the system gets screwy, somehow everyone onboard winds up beaming into puppet versions of themselves. And mostly annoying puppets at that.

I’ve complained about this before, but one of my issues with these Strange New Worlds concept episodes is that a lot of said concepts have been done before, if not ad infinitum , on other shows. The musical episode “Subspace Rhapsody” was great and all, but you know, not exactly an original idea . A film noir episode? Been there. LARPing with the crew? Mmmhmmm . And now we get a puppet episode, the idea of which I can recall seeing at least as far back as on Angel 22 years ago, when it felt like a new idea .

And look, there’s nothing wrong with recycling old premises, but if you’re gonna do it, you gotta bring something new to the table. It’s got to work, and “Level Five Transporter Accident” mostly doesn’t. For starters, by its very nature, the notion of having most of your cast turn into puppets is going to bring a heightened sense of absurdity to things; the characters even harness this idea in their quest to defeat the nasty if forgettable Orion villains of the week. But there’s something about suddenly hearing voices like Anson Mount’s and Christina Chong’s coming from the puppets that I found too jarring. It’s all supposed to be fun and funny, but it’s mostly not, and once again Mount’s take on Pike veers into “this is not a Starfleet captain” territory, wool stuffing notwithstanding.

So what does work here? I think I laughed out loud twice, and both times it was involving the guy at the navigation console next to Ortegas (Melissa Navia) who would usually have been a Red Shirt but instead here is just a funny puppet. His wordless panic about the situation is great. And the puppet designs themselves (created by the Jim Henson Company) are really nice – like, they should sell them on the Paramount+ store because people would want to collect them all. Oh, and the shots near the end of the episode, with the crew all floating around in space in puppet form, are just quite sweet (and really, is how the hour should’ve ended, instead of turning it into an “It was all a dream” scenario for some reason).

And then there’s the Spock stuff, which saves the episode from disaster. Peck’s comedic timing is notable, as he has to run around doing everyone’s jobs for them to keep the ship running, since their little puppet fingers are mostly useless. The actor really has mastered Spock – he and Mount have been playing these characters since 2019 at this point, when they debuted on Star Trek: Discovery – and he always rolls with the various curveballs the writers have thrown at him. Too Vulcan, too human, too Vulcan/human, he’s done it all, and here he’s dealing with not just getting dumped by another crewmate (though La’an was pretty graceful in the dumping, unlike Chapel previously), but also in having to go to his ex, T’Pring (Gia Sandhu), for help in the aftermath of the incident onboard the Griffin earlier this season. I’m glad to see they didn’t just drop that thread, and continuing to explore its impact on both Spock and La’an is welcome.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

About it all being a dream… was it? Little Ricky sure seemed malevolent in that last shot… or maybe Spock just needs more logic training.

But what is this “studying logic” thing anyway? Hasn’t Spock been doing that since he was in diapers?

Could Little Ricky be a reference to the onscreen son of Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz from I Love Lucy? The puppet even has a red crop of hair on its head. Don’t forget, the pair’s production company Desilu was behind the original Star Trek series.

Pelia (Carol Kane) pointing out that they shouldn’t be able to hear each other in space and how it doesn’t even make sense is an appreciated jab at the grumps in the audience like me.

It’s got to work, and “Level Five Transporter Accident” mostly doesn’t. For starters, by its very nature, the notion of having most of your cast turn into puppets is going to bring a heightened sense of absurdity to things; the characters even harness this idea in their quest to defeat the nasty if forgettable Orion villains of the week. But there’s something about suddenly hearing voices like Anson Mount’s and Christina Chong’s coming from the puppets that I found too jarring. It’s all supposed to be fun and funny, but it’s mostly not, and once again Mount’s take on Pike veers into “this is not a Starfleet captain” territory, wool stuffing notwithstanding.

So what does work here? I think I laughed out loud twice, and both times it was involving the guy at the navigation console next to Ortegas (Melissa Navia) who would usually have been a Red Shirt but instead here is just a funny puppet. His wordless panic about the situation is great. And the puppet designs themselves (created by the Jim Henson Company) are really nice – like, they should sell them on the Paramount+ store because people would want to collect them all. Oh, and the shots near the end of the episode, with the crew all floating around in space in puppet form, are just quite sweet (and really, is how the hour should’ve ended, instead of turning it into an “It was all a dream” scenario for some reason).

And then there’s the Spock stuff, which saves the episode from disaster. Peck’s comedic timing is notable, as he has to run around doing everyone’s jobs for them to keep the ship running, since their little puppet fingers are mostly useless. The actor really has mastered Spock – he and Mount have been playing these characters since 2019 at this point, when they debuted on Star Trek: Discovery – and he always rolls with the various curveballs the writers have thrown at him. Too Vulcan, too human, too Vulcan/human, he’s done it all, and here he’s dealing with not just getting dumped by another crewmate (though La’an was pretty graceful in the dumping, unlike Chapel previously), but also in having to go to his ex, T’Pring (Gia Sandhu), for help in the aftermath of the incident onboard the Griffin earlier this season. I’m glad to see they didn’t just drop that thread, and continuing to explore its impact on both Spock and La’an is welcome.
Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:
About it all being a dream… was it? Little Ricky sure seemed malevolent in that last shot… or maybe Spock just needs more logic training.
But what is this “studying logic” thing anyway? Hasn’t Spock been doing that since he was in diapers?

Could Little Ricky be a reference to the onscreen son of Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz from I Love Lucy? The puppet even has a red crop of hair on its head. Don’t forget, the pair’s production company Desilu was behind the original Star Trek series.
Pelia (Carol Kane) pointing out that they shouldn’t be able to hear each other in space and how it doesn’t even make sense is an appreciated jab at the grumps in the audience like me.

articles.title: New Fallout Funko Pops Are Dropping in November, Including Vault Boy, Nuka-Girl, and More
articles.summary: Preorders have dropped for new Fallout Funko Pop figures, which are set to be released this November. Priced at $14.99 a piece, here's where you can secure each figure.
articles.body:
Funko Pop is unleashing some new Fallout figures into the wild this year: Vault Boy , Nuka-Girl , Cappy , and Bottle . Priced at $14.99 a piece, each of these is set to be released in just a few months on November 22, just in time for the holiday season. If you're a big fan of the games (or maybe fell in love with them while watching the TV show ), these look well worth picking up to add to your collectibles.

As is the case with most Funko Pop figures, these are all fairly small (around 3.75 inches tall), so will slot nicely into an existing collection of Fallout-themed goodies. They each have quite fun designs as well.

While Cappy and Bottle are just happily posed with waving hands and big smiles, Nuka-Girl is pictured blasting off in a spacesuit with a ray gun, and Vault Boy is modeled with a classic thumbs up pose and a wink. The latter is a slightly different pose to the Vault Boy Funko Pop that released last year for the TV show , as that one was all wide-eyed smiles while posing instead of the wink.

While their release date isn't until late in November, it's worth preordering these now if one or more of them have caught your eye, rather than waiting. These kinds of figures can sell out faster than you'd think, so it's always a good idea to secure your favorites now before stock is all sold out.

If you're looking for even more Fallout items to buy for your shelves, we've got your covered. Our rundown of the best Fallout gear and collectibles highlights some of our favorite finds we think are worth your time, but the IGN Store is also chock-full of Fallout collectibles to look through. No matter if you've been a longtime fan of the games or just really love the show, there's a little something for everyone.

Hannah Hoolihan is a freelancer who writes with the guides and commerce teams here at IGN.

articles.title: What to Expect from ONL | gamescom 2026
articles.summary: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past and Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will be at gamescom Opening Night Live, but what surprises could be in store? Here's what to expect from ONL on August 25.
articles.body:
It’s that time of year when it's fun to just wildly speculate (and make some educated deductions) about what we might see from Geoff Keighley’s Opening Night Live, direct from gamescom 2026. Little is known ahead of time this year – a few games and studios have been teased, but for the most part the show is a complete mystery, and so this gives me plenty of room to dream about what surprises the show may have in store.

Taking place on August 25 at 11am PT/2pm ET/8pm CEST, here’s how to watch the stream . Let’s not waste any more time, though, and get straight into what to expect from it.

It’s going to be a big night for a couple of the most popular RPGs to ever exist. We’re officially getting our first look at The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past , the third expansion to Geralt’s landmark adventure, coming a whole 12 years after the base game’s release. Co-developed by CD Projekt Red and Fool’s Theory, it’s being described as a prologue of sorts to the upcoming The Witcher 4. Soon, the mystery behind the new, third sword Geralt is holding in the artwork may be revealed, as well as plenty more fans are eager to learn all about, including the expansion’s location and when in The Witcher timeline Songs of the Past is set.

Speaking of old games being revisited, we’ll be getting another look at Final Fantasy 7 Revelation , the last part of Square Enix’s remake trilogy. The project’s director, Naoki Hamaguchi, will be in attendance to show us what’s next for Cloud and the gang, but what exactly could we see? June’s SGF gave us a healthy dose of Highwind action, showing off how we’ll be able to skydive from the iconic airship down to any part of the open world we choose, as well as glimpses into how new party members Vincent Valentine and Cid will control in combat. So, what’s next? Perhaps a deeper dive into one or both of those characters, or maybe a more story-focused sneak peek?

We do know that story is exactly what we’ll be seeing more of from Gears of War: E-Day , though. A brand new trailer for the prequel will be shown at ONL, which will, presumably, include Marcus Fenix slicing up some Locusts. Game of Thrones: War for Westeros will have its gameplay reveal trailer shown off, too. The real-time strategy game puts you in control of one of the fantasy series’ major forces, from the Starks to the Night King’s White Walkers, as you attempt to rewrite Westeros history.

Other games confirmed for the show include Ananta, an upcoming free-to-play open-world game from NetEase that looks to be incorporating all sorts of action into its futuristic city setting. It certainly looks very ambitious, and we’re keen to see more, including, hopefully, a reveal of its release date. Then there’s Ontos, a new sci-fi horror game from Soma and Amnesia studio, Frictional Games. Starring Stellan Skarsgård as one of the occupants of its creepy lunar hotel called Samsara, we’re intrigued to find out more. Action RPG Showa American Story is also set to show up, with a new look at the game that places you in the shoes of a stuntwoman exploring a post-apocalyptic United States. It will be joined by Stage Tour , the rhythm game aiming to pick up where Guitar Hero and Rock Band left off. Then there’s Mewgenics, for which a musical performance is planned on stage. Could some sort of announcement be made for the cat-based tactics game? DLC or a console release, maybe?

The most recent confirmations to be present at the show include Metro 2039 , which, somehow looks like the shooter series’ darkest chapter yet. With it supposedly coming early next year, a good look at gameplay would be welcomed. Also, we know that Tides of Annihilation will be there, presumably with more of that slick-looking combat to show off.

Now for the fun part. What reveals and surprises may await us at ONL? Well, there are a whole host of games coming in September that would presumably love to stand out in the crowd. A big stage like this is the perfect opportunity. These include Marvel’s Wolverine, Control Resonant, Silent Hill: Townfall, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, The Blood of Dawnwalker , and Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave , to name but a few. New trailers for all of these are distinct possibilities.

Moving into October, Call of Duty has somewhat of a tradition of turning up at gamescom to show off a slice of action. Modern Warfare 4 is this year’s offering from Infinity Ward, and is currently available to play in beta. Also due in October is Phantom Blade Zero . We did just get a chunky look at it at the recent State of Play, but we wouldn’t be surprised to see even more of its flashy sword combat here.

Looking beyond this year, Fable is set to be one of 2027’s biggest games, and we’d love another look at Playground Games’ reboot. Even more gameplay would be a treat, especially an insight into the RPG’s combat. We’ve seen a lot of the world and the people living it; now, let’s see how we can kill them.

What other games would you like to see pop up? Perhaps God of War Laufey ? Exodus ? If you’re feeling particularly ambitious, perhaps Persona 6 or the Ocarina of Time remake ? And no, there won’t be any GTA 6. That’s two days later on Netflix.

Let us know in the comments about what you’re most excited about at gamescom’s Opening Night Live show, taking place on August 25, 2026 at 11am PT/2pm ET/8pm CEST.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: This Awesome LEGO-Like Original Xbox Building Kit Is Still Available to Preorder (But It's Sold Out at Amazon)
articles.summary: Mattel has announced a LEGO-like building kit for the original Xbox game console in celebration of its 25th anniversary, but it's selling out fast.
articles.body:
In celebration of Xbox’s 25th anniversary, Mattel Brick Shop has announced a new LEGO-like building kit for a display model of Microsoft’s original Xbox game console. Once assembled, this 3,509-piece set turns into a 1:1 scale model of the device. It includes the console, a hefty full-size Duke controller, and hidden dioramas for three major Xbox games. It looks great, and it’s available for preorder now ( see it at Best Buy ), with a price tag of $329.99 and a release date of October 1 . However, it has already sold out at Amazon , so you may want to buy it sooner than later if you're interested.

Mattel Brick Shop - Microsoft Original Xbox

The console itself looks pretty much just like an original Xbox from 2001. Like like the LEGO Game Boy , the hefty Duke controller has buttons you can press – and when you press them, it triggers interactive lights and sounds in the dioramas hidden inside the console. According to the press release, “Fans can also discover a hidden button combination that triggers an exclusive lighting sequence.” Pretty cool.

The dioramas are worth calling out specifically. Tucked under panels in the console itself are little scenes from three popular Xbox games: Halo: Combat Evolved , The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind , and Psychonauts . (Yes, it's ironic that this is coming out after Microsoft has spun off Psychonauts developer Double Fine Productions). You can keep the dioramas hidden, or you can remove them to display alongside the set.

Additionally, the set comes with 12 “NanoWorld” figures from the games, including Halo’s Master Chief, Psychonauts’ Razputin Aquato, and more.

Formerly known as Mega Bloks, Mattel Brick Shop launched in 2025 as a line of buildable models that come in pieces for you to put together. If that sounds familiar, yes, they’re very similar to LEGO sets . But if the world is big enough for both Coke and Pepsi to co-exist, why not two competing lines of buildable models?

One difference between the two companies is that they’ve courted different brand licenses. LEGO has the likes of Nintendo , Pokémon , Star Wars , and Harry Potter . Mattel, the newer of the two lines, has Masters of the Universe , Hot Wheels , and Xbox. If you’re interested, you can find more Mattel Brick Shop sets here .

Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

articles.title: A Classic Scene From the I Spy Books Has Been Recreated in LEGO
articles.body:
The I Spy book series is a favorite of mine. I collected all of the books as a kid (including the challenge ones!) and have recently started looking at them with my son again. The attention of detail that went into creating each scene is quite incredible and you can always find new things if you look hard enough.

As impressive as the creation of these scenes are, what's even more impressive is that someone has gone ahead and recreated it with only LEGO bricks. Posted in the LEGO Reddit this morning, user burnt-coding shared an image of the scene called "Blocks" from the very first I Spy book.

I recreated an I SPY scene with Lego by u/burnt-coding in lego

Seeing as I own this book myself, I decided to do my own thorough comparison of Walter Wick's original design compared to this brick-built version. And honestly, it's really quite impressively done. The main things that the builder wasn't able to accurately portray were the 11 bears. As indicated in the post, they had to replace the bears with helmets to be able to get close. There's also the three-headed dragon, which seems to have been replaced by three parrots instead. The minifigures don't exactly align with the original figures in the book, but they do get close.

All-in-all, it's a really impressive feat that requires pieces from a ton of different builds. I even recognized the cow and horse figures featured here from LEGO's Duplo Farm set that I recently purchased for my son. This is a MOC that resonates deeply with one of my favorite childhood activities and one of the reasons I love keeping up with the LEGO community. This is the kind of set I would happily buy if it ever got turned into a LEGO Ideas set .

Can You Still Buy the Original I Spy Book?

If you don't still own a copy of the original I Spy book, the good news is that you can still buy the hardcover version on Amazon. It's not the exact same edition I own, but the only difference seems to be slight changes to the cover art. The "Blocks" scene is the first picture riddle featured in this book, and parts of it are also featured in various Challenge books I Spy later released.

Jacob Kienlen is a Senior Audience Development Strategist and Writer for IGN. Born and raised in Portland, Oregon, he has considered the Northwest his home for his entire life. With a bachelor's degree in communication and 10 years of professional writing experience, his expertise is spread across a variety of different pop culture topics -- from TV series to books and the latest LEGO sets .

articles.title: Want a Gears of War Lancer Replica? You Can Preorder One Now
articles.summary: Preorders are live for a full-scale 1:1 Gears of War Prototype Lancer replica, but it'll set you back $300.
articles.body:
I think it’s safe to say that, ever since the original Gears of War hit the Xbox 360 back in 2006, many fans have wanted a lancer of their own. Now that Gears of War E-Day is coming soon, you can have one. An official Gears of War Prototype Lancer Replica is available for preorder on the Xbox Game Studios Shop . It’s not cheap at $299.99, but it’s a full-sized 1:1 scale model, and it looks terrific. Orders placed now are expected to ship in February 2027.

The iconic firearm is an assault rifle that has a chainsaw attached to it, or a “chainsaw bayonet,” if you want to sound elegant. Gears of War E-Day is a prequel to the Gears of War series, depicting the initial alien attack on the planet Sera. As a result, the Lancers used in the game are prototypes of the ones in later installments. Hence the word “prototype” in the name of the replica.

Now this isn’t the first Lancer replica to be released. In fact, we got to go hands-on with one a decade ago around the release of Gears of War 4. But this is the latest one, and it matches the weapons seen in Gears of War E-Day, complete with “a custom, hand-painted battle-worn ‘E-Day' finish that reflects the immediate chaos of the initial strike.”

The replica is full-scale and detailed, and it can be wielded to scare your friends, just like the real thing. But it’s intended to be a display piece, and as such, it comes with a stand and an informational placard so you can set it on your desk or shelf.

Gears of War E-Day comes out October 6, and preorders are live now . You can get a peek at the multiplayer in our first preview of the game.

Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

Gears of War E-Day comes out October 6, and preorders are live now . You can get a peek at the multiplayer in our first preview of the game.
Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

articles.title: The Sinking City 2 Is a Praiseworthy Blend of Lovecraft and Resident Evil
articles.summary: The Sinking City 2 feels inescapably like off-brand Resident Evil, but it's a praiseworthy imitation of its main inspirations wrapped in the Cthulhu mythos.
articles.body:
It was impossible for me to play The Sinking City 2 for more than 15 minutes without coming to the obvious realization that this is Resident Evil in a fedora. That might sound dismissive, but I really enjoy the recent Resident Evil games, so comparing Frogwares' Lovecraftian survival horror sequel to some of the best of them – which feels especially similar to 2019's Resident Evil 2 remake – is much more of a compliment than a put-down. What sets it apart begins with its unique, rich, 1920s New England setting flush with loving detail that instills a strong sense of personality over the top of the mechanics it so clearly imitates.

You play as Calvin Rafferty, a likeable occultist waking up to an apocalyptic flood set to wipe out the entire city of Arkham, Massachusetts in 1929. He's definitely a little bit of a pulp fiction stock character: hard-chinned, two-fisted, and foolishly brave. But there are layers to him that rise to the surface here and there. Similar to the Resident Evil comparison, likening him to the classic heroes of the genre is not really an insult.

The intriguing cosmic horror plot revolves around a half-remembered expedition to Lovecraft's surreal Dreamlands that left Calvin's partner and paramour, Faye, in a comatose state. This creates immediate emotional stakes and momentum from the very start, which carried me through the somewhat slow first half of the first chapter. I don't want to spoil too many surprises, but The Sinking City 2 manages to be a bit of a who's who of the Cthulhu mythos. Some of its eldritch guest characters are much more hinted at than portrayed in all their terrible glory, but Arkham-heads will find lots of little nods to make them cackle with otherworldly glee.

The unfolding story includes some effective emotional beats and a few neat twists that kept me guessing about some characters' motivations, but overall remains pretty easy to follow given the high concept subject matter. This isn't the kind of tale where you're going to have to look up a YouTube video to explain the ending afterwards, and I appreciated that. But it also doesn't back down from engaging with some of the heavier metaphysical aspects of Lovecraft, effectively selling the idea that you're up against beings beyond human comprehension. And it also does a decent job of sidestepping some of the ones that haven't aged particularly well.

The centerpiece is the town of Arkham itself, which presents a gorgeously damp and decrepit backdrop for exploration and combat. Excellent texture work and sound design come together to create an atmosphere that made my skin feel clammy even in the dry heat of a Colorado summer. The density of little details crammed into every corner of every area is truly inspiring. Every dilapidated hotel room or terrifying hospital ward feels both lived-in and ravaged by the ongoing disaster. The cutscenes and facial animations aren't always to the same level of quality, but pretty strong voice acting across the board helps carry them past their production limitations.

Each chapter takes you to a new locale in Arkham, and each feels distinct in both vibes and layout. You start out in the flooded city streets, navigating by boat to various ruins and culminating in a creepy, haunted hotel. Chapter 2, which I found to be the scariest, is set in an abandoned hospital that features its own version of the unkillable stalker in the spirit of Mr. X and Nemesis. And Chapter 3 takes you to the Arkham Fish Market, which goes about exactly how you'd expect if you're familiar with the works of Lovecraft. That is to say, very poorly for our boy Calvin in some unpleasantly fish-themed ways. This progression keeps things fresh while maintaining a cohesive aesthetic.

As I mentioned earlier, when it comes to the mechanics, this is an unapologetic tribute to modern, over-the-shoulder Resident Evil. Calvin can amass a small arsenal of guns, but there are never enough bullets to kill everything, leading to tense scrounging through drawers for every last round. Melee is an option, but not a very effective one. Mixing it up with even your basic zombie-like enemies is almost a guarantee of taking some licks yourself, so close quarters combat became a conscious choice to expend my healing items instead of my ammo. Calvin is not as vulnerable as Resident Evil Requiem's Grace, but he's certainly not a Leon S. Kennedy-level action hero, maintaining a good balance between competent and fragile.

The controls are very similar. The inventory system is very similar. The basic enemies are very similar. There are puzzles where you have to find three things to stick into a door to make it open. You can pick up herbs and craft them into healing items. It even has a system of achievements that unlock powerful perks in New Game+ almost identical to the newer Resident Evil games. Again, I'm not complaining. It's not like I'm sick of the modern Resident Evil formula if it's executed well, and Frogwares did a commendable job, so this feels like a free extra course while we wait for Capcom's next big dish.

One exception to the scarce ammo rule is that certain boss fights or big arena battles have infinitely respawning loot pick-ups (explained by an in-game note that lampshades their bizarre physical properties) to keep you from getting softlocked if your magazines run dry. This felt like a little bit of a cop-out that undermines its difficulty – these segments were some of my least favorite anyway, but hey, you know what else is very Resident Evil? Having boss fights that aren't very good.

All that said, The Sinking City 2 isn't just about Frogwares being a Capcom cover band. One way it sets itself apart is with a perk system that lets you unlock and equip powerful runes that do things like increase your damage when your flashlight is off, rewarding you for being able to hit enemies you can't even see. They come in four tiers of increasing power, and you can't really unlock the strongest ones on a single playthrough, creating a compelling incentive to charge headlong into horror all over again.

The other novel bit is the ability to find written clues around every area that can be organized and connected with red strands like your very own wacky conspiracy board. Each belongs to a group, and correctly connecting each group gives you some progression points. Some give hints on plot-critical objectives, while others point to potent, optional treasures. The rewards feel worthwhile, though some require a little bit of backtracking, even if the puzzles themselves aren't exactly brain-busters.

You can set the difficulty of these puzzles independently of the combat difficulty, which is neat, but all the harder option really does is remove highlighted text and icons that tell you which clues belong together. I didn't find it particularly difficult to figure out which hints were related and put together the information in them myself even without those hints, so it felt like increasing the difficulty from Very Easy to Easy. There is one pretty tough optional puzzle that required me to really use my brain later on, but I did end up yearning for more difficult detective work.

Also, there is no sanity mechanic, which seems a little odd for a Cthulhu game. There are some strange moments of reality-bending theatrics, but I was never made to doubt if the things my character was experiencing were even real. And that's a bit of a letdown.

articles.title: Metal Gear Solid 4: The Flawed Masterpiece Kojima Didn't Want to Make
articles.summary: With Metal Gear Solid 4 finally arriving on modern consoles thanks to Master Collection Vol. 2, we take a look back at the game's legacy. Was it really just a big cutscene, or is it Kojima's masterpiece?
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Charlie Lopresto, who believes that love can bloom, even on a battlefield. He first encountered Metal Gear Solid on a demo disc from Pizza Hut and has since completed three hundred missions in VR– the kind that’s indistinguishable from the real thing.

Like Old Snake, Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots is a fossil. A genetic dead-end of gaming evolution, the unhinged and overflowing masterpiece that barely left a mark on the artform. Despite its commercial and critical success , MGS4 is rarely regarded as top tier Metal Gear. But is that actually fair?

Trapped on dead console hardware for the better part of its hard life, thanks to the new Master Collection Vol. 2 it’s finally possible for everyone to experience MGS4, from series diehards who first fired it up in 2008 to people completely new to Metal Gear who have absolutely no idea what they’re in for.

All of them will reckon with the many, many questions MGS4 brings to mind, like: Will we ever see a game like this again? Why did we stop talking about it? And, perhaps most importantly: MGS4 is really good, isn't it?

Hideo Kojima did not want to make Metal Gear Solid 4. He publicly declared his desire to end the franchise as early as MGS 2, then proclaimed that he was finished with the saga after Snake Eater. Kojima’s words were weary but his deeds said otherwise. He wasn’t really ready to move on– both of those games ooze with a sense of momentum and life.

Guns of the Patriots feels different. There’s a gloomy weight to the game, like a funeral – the raucous kind where friends, grudges, and flames gather to settle scores, awkwardly hook up, and celebrate the end.

Prior to MGS4, we’d last seen Solid Snake in 2001, when he dropped a prophetic monologue and vanished into the streets of lower Manhattan shortly after the former President of the United States crashed into the city with a giant sci-fi submarine. As situations go, it’s certainly one that begs for some followup, and after years of fans demanding the return of the Legendary Mercenary, Kojima obliged in trademark trolling fashion.

You don’t get the cocky, mech-smashing super soldier who slays Tengu by the dozen with a metafictional bandana. Kojima, who reportedly received death threats over his reluctance to move the story forward with MGS4, instead delivers a feeble, actively decomposing relic. Old Snake grunts, screams, coughs and gags wetly as he crawls in agony through his final mission, all for the privilege of being allowed to die before his poisoned blood wipes out humanity. Old Snake was punished before Punished was cool.

It’s a trope we’ve seen a lot lately: the beloved hero of a bygone age, bitter, broken down, and humbled, all in service of passing the torch to a spunky new recruit before the credits roll. But there is no Rey to don the cardboard box here, no Adonis Creed, no Robin, nor any kind of chipper next-gen protagonist queued to continue Snake’s legacy by selling some video games. Nearly everyone in Metal Gear Solid 4 is old, dead, or extremely married by the end of the story, a bittersweet and beautifully conclusive eulogy to a deeply heroic and thoroughly decrepit old man who reeks of cigarettes.

Modern media is designed to protect itself, to keep mythology marketable and leave endings open for future exploitation. Kojima does the exact opposite with MGS4, performing peaceful euthanasia on his life’s work to that point. It’s a brave move delivered with a lot of love and earnestness, and anyone upset at geriatric Snake were too busy feasting on a buffet of fanservice to stay mad for long.

Rarely do sprawling stories wrap up as neatly as Metal Gear Solid’s, even if “neatly” here means bursting at the seams and slightly slapdash. Kojima didn’t have a decades-long master plan when he made Metal Gear for the MSX in 1987, but managed to B.S. his way into satisfying answers for nearly everything. It’s an ambitious, messy, and sincere sendoff to Snake and the series. There’s really nowhere else to go from here.

Which brings us to the elephant in the room, dangling precariously from a Fulton balloon over this discussion: Guns of the Patriots is not the last Metal Gear Solid game. Despite his protestations, Kojima had two more Metal Gears in him: the portable Peace Walker, a numbered entry in all but name, and the tragic MGS5. Both respect the brick wall he built at the end of the timeline and tread water safely in the past instead of pushing forward. Kojima decided to move the series horizontally instead, experimenting with tech and form until Konami kicked him out.

Kojima’s actual final chapter, when it came, was compromised and ignominious, a casualty of his ugly exit from Konami and a sour note on which to end. Guns of the Patriots was Kojima ending things on his own terms; a bombastic epic with a massive budget that bursts with supreme confidence and unfiltered honesty. It would be the last time he ever made a game like this.

Guns of the Patriots, like every mainline Metal Gear game before it, is structured like a linear, cinematic action-adventure story. It’s almost quaint from a 2026 lens, when half the industry runs on open worlds and the other on live-service menuslop, but this was Kojima’s M.O. throughout the early part of his career.

And yet for something so committed to telling one continuous story in agonizing detail, MGS4 feels oddly episodic. Each of its five acts is practically a different genre. One minute you’re scooching across a battlefield, then next you’re skulking through the streets of Eastern Europe in a trenchcoat. Kojima drops us into warzones and weapons facilities across the globe, introduces new ideas, and moves past them just as quickly.

A much-hyped faction loyalty system stops mattering after Act 2, and the mechanic to manipulate enemy emotions isn’t really a factor until New Game Plus. There are a whopping 70 guns available for Snake that are largely superfluous, while the omnipresent Psyche meter quickly fades into the background outside of some perfectly-timed comedy. It’s like Kojima is cramming every single cockamamie “Metal Gear” idea he had left into the game as if it were his last chance, or so he hoped.

Kojima’s Hollywood aspirations run wild here, and while some of the sloggier cinematics are a chore, I’d sit through a thousand torturous mission briefings to relive MGS4’s queasy, white-knuckle fusions of story and mechanics, like the sicko mode split screen action setpieces and the tactile desperation of the microwave hallway.

The game’s linearity is a huge strength. We embody Old Snake through every second of his grueling ordeal. We wince with every injury and every brutal negging. Solid Snake was our stand-in from the moment he infiltrated Outer Heaven, detours aside, and we feel every moment of the long journey as he slugs it out with “Liquid” one last time. That sense of embodiment, being inside Snake, a part of him… you can’t get that from a mission select screen. But Kojima’s next and last games in his Metal Gear Solid saga would be built with these impersonal menus in mind.

Frustrated with the PS3’s limitations for his grand scale vision, Kojima went small instead. Also available in Master Collection Vol. 2, Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker was originally built for the handheld Playstation Portable, so a sprawling linear opus was pretty much off the table without the luxury of blu-ray discs and Cell processors. Instead, he designed for the handheld system’s strengths: short, snackable stealth missions selected from a menu, perfect for a train ride or waiting room.

Previous Metal Gears relied on blockbuster storytelling to keep you coming back, but Peace Walker leans on moreish base-building, optional challenges, and RPG systems borrowed from Monster Hunter to keep you hooked. Seven years after Snake bluntslid across the Big Shell, grinding was back in Metal Gear, and this time it was here to stay.

Kojima is clearly fond of the results. He considers Peace Walker the fifth mainline MGS game, and thanks to rereleases it’s had far more staying power than the average PSP game. He liked the formula so much that he made it his default going forward: both MGS5 and the Death Stranding games run on the same skeleton, embracing timers and stats and judging your performance in isolated missions chosen from a list. At this rate we’ll probably be chasing S-ranks in OD.

It works beautifully for a handheld, and for a taciturn cipher like Sam Bridges, but it really doesn’t suit traditional Metal Gear Solid. MGS5 was free from the shackles of a 272p screen, but even with the full glory of the Fox Engine, the menu-driven mode of interaction keeps us at arms length from Snake.

The story becomes another checklist item, grinding through side ops until an actually important mission appears on the list. We’re watching from a more omniscient remove as Snake sizes up the stats of future subordinates and navigates a tech tree. For a series that loves to mess directly with the player and collapse the space between them and the character, losing that intimacy comes with a cost. MGS4 made Snake’s suffering feel like ours, and the series never approached that level of pathos again.

Being inside Old Snake’s head for dozens of hours is genuinely unpleasant at times, to the point it makes the game almost hard to revisit, and it’s one of several reasons why MGS4’s legacy is so quiet.

It’s hard for a game to have an ongoing influence when nobody can play it. Metal Gear Solid 4 has been unavailable for years, buried alive on hardware that Sony hasn’t sold for nearly a decade. Countless classic titles are trapped on ancient tech, but it’s rare for a numbered entry in a massive, triple A series.

The PS3’s Cell Processor was notoriously miserable to develop for, with bizarre architecture far removed from industry standards that made porting anything off it a nightmare. It’s also why emulation, so vital to keeping commercially abandoned games alive, couldn’t save Old Snake either. Strides have been made recently, but MGS4 remains a genuine bear to run outside of its native hardware.

None of these technical woes were insurmountable, and neither were the super specific Sony references or the licensing entanglements from MGS4’s frankly ludicrous product placement. It just needed a publisher that cared enough to devote the resources to porting it and had the courage to get Uniqlo, Apple, and Playboy back to the negotiating table.

Konami was content to let the series languish for a long time as it explicitly abandoned video games for pachinko parlors. It only once really wrestled with following MGS4 in the timeline, in Platinum’s audacious spinoff Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance . Otherwise, it didn’t matter to Konami if nobody could buy or play MGS4.

Thankfully, that’s changed. Konami’s prodigal return to video games has gone well enough so far, and now MGS4 is enjoying an immaculate rebirth, iPod and all. How will modern gamers receive it after so many years in the wilderness?

Guns of the Patriots is an aggressively unfriendly game by modern standards, and the cutscenes are completely out of control. A common Kojima criticism is that he’d rather make movies than games, but it’s hard to think of any film that’s nine hours long, built largely out of static codec calls, and features extended scenes of people drinking soda and smoking around little girls while weeping about nanomachines and infectious diseases. Whatever MGS4 is, it’s not a movie, and it’s certainly not made for newcomers.

MGS4 isn’t spoken of in the same breath as the first three games, and when it does come up it’s rarely for what it actually accomplished. And since almost nobody’s been able to play the game for so long, its reputation as an uncomfortable cutscene parade is all that remains. Opinion calcifies when there’s nothing around to contradict it.

That’s not to say nobody’s tried to pick up what MGS4 put down. Resident Evil Requiem almost feels like a tribute at times, a last ride for a long-suffering hero who makes a pilgrimage back to where his story started while dying from a sci-fi disease that makes him cough a lot. By the end, Leon is upgrading his weapons with counterfeit Drebin Points, dueling hand-to-hand with his longtime rival, and dragging himself inch by agonizing inch through a high-tech hallway.

Without spoiling where it lands, Requiem doesn’t have the nerve to go out on a limb like MGS4. Its tribute to Raccoon City sent us on a nostalgic trip through a place we’ve already walked through twice in HD, stopping far short of the wobbly PSX vertices in MGS4’s homage to Shadow Moses, another holy gaming space introduced in 1998. The ending stops short as well, a clean cut affair that leaves plenty of room for further adventures and profitable sequels.

Triple-A gaming didn’t go in an MGS4 direction in the intervening years. Budgets are too big and bosses too demanding to allow a freakazoid like Kojima off the leash again– unless you’re the man himself, of course. But Kojima only gets away with that because he had the power to leave the system that made MGS4 possible. Everyone else is still answering to a spreadsheet and, understandably, gunshy about unfettered visionaries.

Modern gaming’s play-it-safe instincts could do wonders for MGS4’s reputation. George Lucas and his Star Wars prequels suffered a similar rap over the years, dismissed as the bloated self-indulgent work of an auteur no one could rein in. But a decade of focus-tested corpo Star Wars sequels has sparked a genuine re-evaluation of the much-maligned Episodes I, 2, and 3, and now that it’s available again, MGS4 deserves the same treatment. Both the prequels and MGS4 are messy, overstuffed, and often embarrassing, but they are never once indifferent. Sincerity ages a lot better than caution.

Ultimately, everyone has to judge Metal Gear Solid 4 for themselves, to witness the grandiosity, endure the hour-plus uninterrupted cutscenes, and gaze hypnotically at Old Snake’s buttcheeks amidst a bombardment of jargon and lore. At least now you’ll get the chance to, and when you do finally sit with Kojima’s wayward masterpiece, you might like it more than you’d think.

Charlie "Moose" Lopresto graduated law school, passed the bar, and made a financially questionable decision to write about games and movies instead. Contributing to IGN since 2021, he collects solo board games and transforming robots.
